description: About Tritium Fuel Cycle (TFC) GFG is designing a first-of-a-kind (FOAK) fusion power plant (FPP) to deliver 1 GW of electrical power in the 2040s. The “GIGA” plant will be based on a stellarator magnetic confinement fusion device, operating continuously on a deuterium-tritium (D-T) fuel cycle. Prior to this, the smaller “Gauss Industrial Demonstrator (GID-170)” will be deployed in the mid-2030s. While deuterium can be extracted from seawater, tritium is a tightly controlled radioactive isotope with an extremely limited global supply. Therefore, both GID-170 and GIGA must utilise closed tritium fuel cycle infrastructure, to ensure that unburnt tritium is fully recycled back to the stellarator and not released to the environment. Meanwhile, the tritium consumed by the fusion reaction must be replenished using tritium breeding blankets (TBB). A first-of-a-kind dedicated tritium fuel cycle (TFC) facility, suitable for continuously supporting a stellarator device, must be designed, built and commissioned. It will adopt a multi-loop process architecture, each loop comprising many deeply integrated subsystems. Developing such a facility presents unique engineering challenges: the supply chain is still emerging, commercial process simulation tools lack dedicated TFC libraries, suitable off-the-shelf equipment is not always available, and some technologies have relatively low technology readiness levels (TRLs). A conceptual design is currently under development, with the project then progressing into pre-front-end engineering design (pre-FEED) in 2028, followed by front-end engineering design (FEED) and design for manufacturing phases. Completion of the overall design phase (for GID-170) must be achieved by 2032. About the role GFG is looking for several Tritium Process Engineers to join the TFC department and develop the GID-170 and GIGA TFC facilities. The roles will contribute to the continued development and optimisation of the overall fuel cycle architecture and its subsystems. Activities will include managing design requirements; developing process flow diagrams (PFDs), piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs), heat and mass balances (HMBs) and the Basis of Design (BoD); selecting technologies; sizing and arranging equipment; and contributing to safety-related design. The roles may also involve supporting equipment prototype development and testing with technology developers and research partners. We welcome candidates with complementary strengths in process design and process modelling and simulation, with systems engineering experience also desirable. These specialisations sit within the same engineering function, and candidates are not expected to have equal expertise across all areas. Each engineer will contribute across several activities and will be expected to take ownership of specific tasks or subsystems, or lead work packages, depending on their experience. The roles will involve close collaboration with engineers from the same and other disciplines at national and international partner organisations, research institutions and suppliers, as well as with colleagues across disciplines and departments within GFG. Given the specific challenges associated with tritium, close collaboration with Nuclear Safety and Export Control specialists will also be essential. During conceptual design, successful candidates will work closely with the Head of Tritium Fuel Cycle to address the strong interdependencies between subsystems and develop a coherent, integrated design. As the project moves into pre-FEED, they will be expected to take greater day-to-day ownership of their assigned areas and drive design development through pre-FEED and FEED, while maintaining close coordination across subsystem interfaces. As the project progresses, the roles will evolve to support design for manufacture, procurement and commissioning of the GID-170 TFC systems, followed by further development and refinement of the TFC design for GIGA. Support the development and integration of custom models and, where appropriate, contribute to the development of dedicated simulation tools. Cost, safety and risk management Identify and manage design risks, developing effective risk-reduction strategies and action plans. Identify applicable standards, regulations and codes, and ensure that these are considered throughout the design process. Participate in hazard, safety and accident analyses, including hazard identification (HAZID) and hazard and operability (HAZOP) studies, and contribute to the definition of safety functions and development of the safety case. Contribute to capital and operational expenditure (CAPEX/OPEX) estimates. Design development and delivery Develop design documentation and specifications, including contributions to the Basis of Design and design philosophies. Document design studies, verification and assessment activities, engineering assumptions and design decisions. Support the design development, procurement and testing of prototypes for key components, in collaboration with technology developers, suppliers and research partners. Provide engineering support for R&D activities conducted in-house and with external partners and collaborators. Project coordination and collaboration Lead specific technical tasks or work packages assigned by the Head of TFC, in line with experience and expertise. Take ownership of specific subsystems throughout the pre-FEED and FEED studies, as assigned by the Head of TFC, in line with experience and expertise. Participate in technical meetings with partners, suppliers, research institutions and other collaborators. Collaborate closely with other engineering disciplines and contribute to the integration of TFC systems within the wider fusion plant. Specialist Skills Candidates are expected to demonstrate strengths in one or more of the following areas, depending on their background and specialisation. description: quinn is becoming the way people employ, across the globe, through one app. quinn is an app-based, managed payroll and employment-administration service. We run it for private households employing a cleaner, nanny, or caretaker, and for businesses that manage employment relationships at scale. The customer stays the legal employer: quinn registers the employment, runs payroll, and handles social insurance, taxes, and filings on their behalf, automated end to end. Where everyone else sells software, quinn sells the outcome. We don't sell payroll software. We run payroll. The purpose behind it is simple: Fair employment. For all. Correct and fair employment, made simple and accessible for any employer and any employee, in any market quinn enters. Where this is going Think about what Revolut did to banking. All of the complexity (the regulation, the clearing, the compliance) handled invisibly in the background, and one simple experience at the front. Nobody using Revolut thinks about what happens behind the screen when they open a new account, swap currencies or send money abroad. It just works, in a couple of taps. Nobody should have to think about it in order to employ someone either. That is what quinn is building, and it is further along than most people assume: a profitable core business, running today in Switzerland, Germany and the UK, expanding into new markets both by launching and by acquiring. By 2030 quinn intends to be the destination brand for fair employment across six countries and more, on one platform, with one experience. One platform means one frontend. One experience means it looks and behaves like quinn whether you are in Zurich or in London, a household or a company. In this strategy that is not a nice-to-have. It is the strategy. Which is why the surface matters more than anything else. Everything quinn does is designed to disappear. The interface is the only part the customer ever sees, and it is the whole proof that the complexity behind it is really handled. Why this role exists Today , quinn runs on several separate web apps: one per product and market, each with its own frontend, grown over the years as the company grew. Our backend engineers built them alongside everything else, plus an internal admin tool that grew the same way. They all work: thousands of employers run payroll through them every month. But nobody was ever tasked with owning the frontend development, so each one got built the way frontend is built by Backend Developers, seen as a hassle rather than the main aspect users interactive with. What comes next is one frontend that replaces all of them, built from scratch: one quinn app for employers, employees and our own support team, in the browser first, then in the App Store and Google Play from the same work. Alongside it, the frontend of Maestro, the internal tool that replaces the old admin for batch processes. The phone app is the surface that matters most, so everything is built for it from the first screen rather than adapted to it afterwards. That is the opening. How we work We are AI-native, and we mean it operationally rather than as a slogan. AI is how the work gets done here. It is why a small team ships like a large one, and it is a large part of how one person will be able to hold the standard we are describing. We expect you to be at the front of that. Not to have heard of the tools, to live in them, and to build your own leverage with them: scaffolding, visual regression checks, design-token pipelines, whatever takes manual work out of the way. And we expect the judgement that has to come with it. AI writes code that looks right and is subtly wrong: structure that doesn't scale, patterns that fall apart three screens later, components that work once and never again. You take the speed and throw away the rest. AI never lowers the bar here. It is the reason the bar can be this high. Tasks What you will own Everything on the screen: The frontend of the quinn app and the web app. App first. One app for everyone who uses quinn: the employer, the employee, and our own support team working inside the customer's account. The frontend of Maestro, our internal batch tool. Desktop and dense: queues, runs, tables, filters, multi-select, keyboard shortcuts. A different discipline from the app, built on the same components. The component library across quinn Home and quinn Business: one frontend, one experience, every market and every device. Whether the app feels native: response, scrolling, gestures, transitions, biometric login, push. Nothing that gives away it isn't native. The quality of what you ship. Nothing leaves your hands half-finished. Where design ends, engineering begins. We have a design team, and they own how quinn looks and behaves: the flows, the visual design, the tokens, the component specs. You don't design. You own everything from there: how it is built, and everything a design file cannot reasonably specify, such as gestures, keyboard, safe areas, what happens between the drawn breakpoints, the loading, offline, pending and failed states, what a three-line German label does to a layout that was designed for English. You are in the room before design starts, saying what already exists in the library and what a new pattern costs. Not at the end, receiving a handover. When you and design disagree, they decide how it looks and behaves and you decide how it is built. Nothing enters the component library without both of you. Requirements Who we are looking for You care about interfaces more than anyone else in the room. You see the two-pixel misalignment without being told, and it bothers you until it is fixed. You build and maintain UI components and design systems, not one-off screens. You can build a mobile app that feels like one. And you can also build a desktop tool full of tables, filters and keyboard shortcuts, because Maestro is one. You understand UX and how people actually behave, not only how a screen looks. And you write code other people can take over: scalable, structured, documented. Not something that only works while you are in the building. You are independent and decisive. Nobody will spec every detail for you and nobody will review your pixels. You are fluent in English, no other language is required. And if you have a portfolio, a live product, or anything you have shipped that you are proud of, show it to us. Not a requirement, but it tells us more than a CV does. Most importantly: you want this one. Not a frontend role at a company where the frontend is a chore. This one, the app nobody has built yet, the standard nobody has set yet, and a company where getting it right actually decides whether the strategy works. The Team We are a small, fast, direct team. We do not have a lot of process or a lot of hierarchy. We do have a clear strategy, an ambitious plan, and five values we actually mean: Be open, Own it, Speak up, Keep it simple, Bias for action. This is one of the most important hires we will make this year. We are not rushing it and we are not filling a seat. We are looking for the person who reads this and thinks: finally. description: About Us Harmattan AI is a next-generation defense prime building autonomous and scalable defense systems. About the Role As a Mechatronics Engineer Intern on the Flight Autonomy team, you will design and program an automated calibration bench for the sensors on our autonomous systems. The bench will be replicated for production, so it must be reliable, documented and usable without you. This internship may lead to a full-time position. Responsibilities Learn our robotic systems, onboard sensors and current calibration process before building on it. Develop sensor calibration workflows for sensors like IMUs, cameras and magnetometers. Program the robotic arm to move sensors through repeatable, automated calibration sequences. Build automated data capture, processing and reporting that produce calibration files ready to load. Design and make mounts, fixtures and calibration targets for the bench. Collect and analyse sensor data on the bench and on real systems to validate results. Document the bench so sensor engineers can run it on their own and it can be replicated for production. Work closely with sensor and navigation engineers and review progress regularly with your supervisor. Candidate Requirements Final-year Master’s or engineering school student in robotics, computer science, mechatronics, microengineering or a related field. Clean, well-structured Python; C++ is a plus. Experience automating the processing of sensor or measurement data. Working knowledge of camera models and IMUs, or hands-on experience calibrating a sensor. Experience designing simple mechanical parts such as mounts and fixtures and getting them made. Experience building test setups that give repeatable results, and debugging them methodically. Experience on a drone, Formula Student, rocketry or robotics student team is a plus. Hands-on, autonomous and rigorous, with a track record of building things that work. We look forward to hearing how you can help shape the future of autonomous defense systems at Harmattan AI. A freight forwarder runs that whole journey, so the brand that makes the goods doesn't have to.</p> <p>Most forwarders still run it on email, spreadsheets and phone calls. Our agents handle 21 million tasks a year, and up to 80% of customs work is automated.</p> <p>Global logistics is a $13 trillion industry, and even the largest forwarder earns less than 3% of global logistics outsourcing revenue. Self-driving cars are rated from level 0 to level 5. Most of the freight industry still runs at level 0: people emailing spreadsheets. Our goal is level 5 for freight, with Forge as the best agentic platform there is, handling every complexity, every calamity and every odd preference without skipping a beat.</p> <p><strong>Stack:</strong> TypeScript, Rust, Next.js, Temporal, Postgres and Snowflake, with models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.</p> <h2>The role</h2> <p>As an Applied AI Engineer II on Autonomous Supply Chains, you'll build the agents and AI-powered applications that make Flexport's operations faster and increasingly autonomous.
